meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.stem: Which expression equals ln(2 × 5)?

options.feedback: Logs turn products into sums, not into products of logs: ln(2) × ln(5) ≈ 0.693 × 1.609 ≈ 1.12, but ln(10) ≈ 2.30.
Correct. The product rule says ln(ab) = ln(a) + ln(b), so ln(10) = 0.693 + 1.609 ≈ 2.30.

options.text: ln(7)
options.feedback: ln(7) is the log of the sum 2 + 5, not of the product 2 × 5.
2 × ln(5) = ln(5²) = ln(25) by the power rule, not ln(10).

practice.explanation: Section 9.1 (product rule): ln(ab) = ln(a) + ln(b). Logs convert multiplication into addition, which is why multiplicative relationships become linear in logs.

practice.stem: Which statements about the natural logarithm are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: ln(a − b) = ln(a) − ln(b) for any a > b > 0.
options.feedback: There is no rule for the log of a difference. For example, ln(10 − 5) = ln(5) ≈ 1.61, while ln(10) − ln(5) ≈ 0.69.

options.text: ln(10) is approximately 2.30.
options.feedback: Correct: e^2.30 ≈ 10, as the chapter's table of ln(x) values shows.

options.text: ln(x) increases as x increases.
options.feedback: Correct: ln(x) is an increasing function, although it rises more and more slowly as x grows.

options.text: ln(a) × ln(b) = ln(a + b) for any a, b > 0.
options.feedback: Neither products nor sums of logs work this way; the product rule links ln(ab) to the sum ln(a) + ln(b).

options.text: ln(x) is defined only for x > 0.
options.feedback: Correct: the natural logarithm exists only for positive numbers, which is why variables with zeros or negative values cannot be logged.

practice.explanation: Section 9.1: ln(x) is defined for x > 0, increasing, and turns products into sums. There is no simple rule for the log of a difference.

practice.stem: Doubling a positive number x raises ln(x) by the same amount, whatever the starting value of x.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. ln(2x) = ln(2) + ln(x), so doubling always adds ln(2) ≈ 0.693.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the product rule in Section 9.1: ln(2x) = ln(2) + ln(x).

practice.explanation: Section 9.1: ln(2x) = ln(2) + ln(x), so doubling always adds ln(2) ≈ 0.693 to the log. A constant proportionate change is a constant change in logs.

practice.concept: Logarithmic approximation of proportionate change (Section 9.1, Key Concept 9.1)
practice.stem: Suppose a price rises from 100 to 110, a 10% increase. Using 100 × [ln(110) − ln(100)], what percentage change would you compute, and how does it compare with the exact change?

options.text: About 10.0%, equal to the exact change
options.feedback: The log difference is ln(1.1) ≈ 0.0953, not 0.10. The approximation is close for a 10% change but not exact.

options.text: About 0.095%, below the exact 10% change
options.feedback: 0.0953 is the proportionate change; multiply by 100 to express it as a percentage.

options.text: About 10.5%, above the exact 10% change
options.feedback: 10.5% is 100 × (e^0.10 − 1), which converts a log change of 0.10 into an exact percentage. Here the log change is ln(1.1), not 0.10.

options.text: About 9.5%, slightly below the exact 10% change
options.feedback: Correct: 100 × ln(1.1) ≈ 9.53%, slightly below the exact 10%.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.1: 100 × Δln(x) ≈ %Δx, and the approximation is good for changes up to about 10%. For an increase, the log change is a little smaller than the exact percentage change.

practice.stem: Section 9.2 gives the example of a price elasticity of demand equal to −2. What does this mean?

options.text: A $1 rise in price lowers the quantity demanded by 2 units.
options.feedback: That is a slope in levels (units per dollar). An elasticity relates percentage changes to percentage changes.

options.text: A 1% rise in price lowers the quantity demanded by 0.02%.
options.feedback: The elasticity is already a ratio of percentage changes; it is not divided by 100.

options.text: A 1% rise in price lowers the quantity demanded by about 2%.
options.feedback: Correct. An elasticity of −2 means the quantity demanded changes by about −2% for each 1% change in price.

options.text: A 2% rise in price lowers the quantity demanded by about 1%.
options.feedback: This reverses the ratio. The elasticity divides the % change in quantity by the % change in price.

practice.explanation: Section 9.2: elasticity = (Δy/y)/(Δx/x), the percentage change in y for a 1% change in x. An elasticity of −2 means a 1% price rise is associated with about a 2% fall in quantity.

practice.stem: Suppose a study finds that a 1% rise in household income is associated with a 0.6% rise in restaurant spending, and that each additional child in a household is associated with 4% lower restaurant spending. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The income elasticity of restaurant spending is about 0.6.
options.feedback: Correct: a percentage change in spending per percentage change in income is an elasticity.

options.text: The semi-elasticity of restaurant spending with respect to the number of children is about −0.04.
options.feedback: Correct: a proportionate change in spending (−0.04) per one-unit change in children is a semi-elasticity.

options.text: The income figure is a semi-elasticity, because income is measured in dollars.
options.feedback: What matters is how the change in x is expressed: income changes by 1%, a proportionate change, so this is an elasticity.

options.text: A 10% rise in income is associated with about 6% higher restaurant spending.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.2: a semi-elasticity is a proportionate change in y per unit change in x; an elasticity is a proportionate change in y per proportionate change in x. Children are counted in units; income changes are expressed in percent.

practice.stem: Practice Exercise 2 uses the log-linear model ln(wage) = 1.50 + 0.085 × experience, with the hourly wage in dollars and experience in years. Which interpretation of 0.085 is correct?

options.text: Each additional year of experience is associated with an hourly wage about 8.5% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-linear model, 100 × b is the approximate percentage change in y for a one-unit increase in x.

options.text: Each additional year of experience raises the hourly wage by about $8.50.
options.feedback: The dependent variable is ln(wage), so the slope describes a proportionate change, not a dollar amount.

options.text: The hourly wage of a worker with no experience is about 8.5% of the average wage.
options.feedback: That would concern the intercept. The slope describes how ln(wage) changes as experience rises.

options.text: A worker with 1% more experience earns an hourly wage about 8.5% higher.
options.feedback: Experience enters in years, not in logs, so the slope is a semi-elasticity: it refers to one more year, not to 1% more experience.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.3: in ln(y) = β₀ + β₁x, 100 × β₁ ≈ the percentage change in y when x rises by one unit. Here: about 8.5% per year of experience.

practice.stem: In the same wage model (slope 0.085), five more years of experience change ln(wage) by 5 × 0.085 = 0.425. What is the exact percentage change in the predicted wage?

options.feedback: This is the approximation 100 × 0.425. For a log change this large it understates the exact change.
e^0.425 − 1 ≈ 0.53 is a proportionate change; multiply by 100 to express it in percent.
This is 100 × e^0.425 without subtracting 1. The exact formula is 100 × (e^Δln(y) − 1).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.1: for large log changes use the exact formula %Δy = 100 × (e^Δln(y) − 1). Here 100 × (e^0.425 − 1) ≈ 53.0%, well above the 42.5% approximation.

practice.stem: In the model ln(wage) = 1.50 + 0.085 × experience, one more year of experience is associated with a larger predicted dollar raise for a worker whose predicted wage is $40 per hour than for one whose predicted wage is $20 per hour.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The model implies the same percentage raise (about 8.5%) for both, which is about $3.40 at $40 per hour but about $1.70 at $20 per hour.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the remark in Key Concept 9.3 that a percentage interpretation 'scales automatically'.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.3: a log-linear model implies a constant percentage effect, so the dollar effect grows with the wage level: 8.5% of $40 is about $3.40 and 8.5% of $20 is about $1.70.

practice.stem: Suppose that in the wage model the slope 0.085 has a two-sided p-value of 0.04 for H₀: β₁ = 0. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: There is a 4% probability that the true slope is zero.
options.feedback: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it is not the probability that H₀ is true.

options.text: The null hypothesis of a zero slope is rejected at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Correct. p = 0.04 < 0.05, so H₀ is rejected at 5%. Significance describes an association; by itself it does not show that experience causes higher wages.

options.text: The slope is not statistically significant, because 0.085 is much smaller than 1.
options.feedback: Significance depends on the estimate relative to its standard error, not on whether the estimate is above 1.

options.text: Each year of experience raises wages by about 4%, the size of the p-value.
options.feedback: The p-value is a probability about the test, not an effect size. The effect size comes from the slope.

practice.explanation: Section 9.3 reports t-statistics and p-values for log models just as for linear ones. A p-value below 0.05 means the slope is significant at the 5% level; it measures evidence against H₀, not the size of the effect or causation.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of a firm's output on its capital stock gives ln(output) = 1.2 + 0.7 × ln(capital). Which interpretation of 0.7 is correct?

options.text: Each additional unit of capital raises output by 0.7 units.
options.feedback: Both variables are in logs, so the slope relates percentage changes, not units.

options.text: A 1% increase in capital is associated with about 0.7% higher output.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-log model the slope is the elasticity: the percentage change in y for a 1% change in x.

options.text: A 1% increase in capital is associated with about 70% higher output.
options.feedback: The slope of a log-log model is already in percent-per-percent terms; it is not multiplied by 100.

options.text: Each additional unit of capital raises output by about 0.7%.
options.feedback: That would be a semi-elasticity, which comes from a log-linear model where capital enters in levels.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.4: in ln(y) = β₀ + β₁ln(x), β₁ is the elasticity: a 1% increase in x is associated with about a β₁% change in y. Here 0.7 < 1.

practice.stem: Suppose a log-log model relates a firm's sales to its number of employees, and a firm has 250 employees. A '1% increase in employees' corresponds to how many additional employees for this firm?

options.text: 1 employee
options.feedback: One employee is a one-unit change. A 1% change depends on the starting level: 1% of 250.

options.text: 25 employees
options.feedback: 25 employees is 10% of 250.

options.text: 0.25 employees
options.feedback: 0.25 employees is 0.1% of 250.

options.text: 2.5 employees
options.feedback: Correct: 1% of 250 is 0.01 × 250 = 2.5 employees.

practice.explanation: Section 9.3 notes that a '1% increase' in a variable measured in natural units can be artificial: its size in units depends on the starting level (here 0.01 × 250 = 2.5 employees).

practice.stem: Suppose a log-log model gives an elasticity of sales with respect to advertising of 0.5, with advertising measured in thousands of dollars. Approximately what percentage gain in sales does one more thousand dollars of advertising bring for a firm spending 25 thousand and for one spending 50 thousand?

options.text: About 2% at 25 thousand and about 1% at 50 thousand
options.feedback: Correct: one more thousand is a 4% rise at 25 and a 2% rise at 50; times 0.5 gives about 2% and 1%.

options.text: About 0.5% at both spending levels
options.feedback: 0.5% is the gain from a 1% rise in advertising. One more thousand is a different percentage rise at each level.

options.text: About 1% at 25 thousand and about 2% at 50 thousand
options.feedback: One more thousand is a larger percentage rise for the firm that spends less, so its sales gain in percent is larger.

options.text: About 12.5% at 25 thousand and about 25% at 50 thousand
options.feedback: This multiplies the elasticity by the spending level. The percentage rise in advertising is 100 × 1 ÷ spending.

practice.explanation: Section 9.3: in a log-log model the percentage effect of a one-unit increase in x is about 100 × β₁ / x, which falls as x rises: 100 × 0.5/25 = 2% and 100 × 0.5/50 = 1%.

practice.stem: In the model ln(wage) = 1.50 + 0.085 × experience, the coefficient would stay 0.085 if experience were measured in months instead of years.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what a semi-elasticity measures in Section 9.2: a change per unit of x. Ask what happens when the unit of x changes.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. A semi-elasticity is a change per unit of x. One month is 1/12 of a year, so the coefficient would become about 0.085/12 ≈ 0.0071.

practice.explanation: Section 9.2: the semi-elasticity (Δy/y)/Δx depends on the units of x. Measuring experience in months divides the coefficient by 12.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of a household's annual spending on recreation (in dollars) gives spending = 200 + 3,000 × ln(income). Approximately how much does recreation spending change when income rises by 1%?

options.text: About $3,000
options.feedback: β₁ is the change in y for a one-unit change in ln(x), which is about a 100% change in x. For 1%, divide by 100.

options.text: About 30% more spending
options.feedback: Spending is measured in dollars, not in logs, so the effect is a dollar amount, not a percentage.

options.text: About $30
options.feedback: Correct: in a linear-log model, a 1% increase in x changes y by about β₁/100 = 3,000/100 = $30.

options.text: About $300
options.feedback: This divides by 10 instead of 100. A 1% change in x changes ln(x) by about 0.01.

practice.explanation: Section 9.2 and Model 4 in Section 9.3: in y = β₀ + β₁ln(x), Δy ≈ (β₁/100) × %Δx. Here a 1% rise in income adds about $30 of recreation spending.

practice.stem: In the recreation model spending = 200 + 3,000 × ln(income), how does the predicted dollar increase in spending from a 1% rise in income change as income rises?

options.text: It stays the same: about $30 at every income level.
options.feedback: Correct: a 1% rise in income raises ln(income) by about 0.01 at any income level, so spending rises by about 3,000 × 0.01 = $30 everywhere.

options.text: It stays at $3,000 at every income level, the slope coefficient.
options.feedback: The slope is the change for a one-unit change in ln(income), roughly a 100% rise in income. A 1% rise gives about 1/100 of it.

options.text: It rises, since 1% of a higher income is more dollars of income.
options.feedback: Spending depends on ln(income), and a 1% rise changes ln(income) by the same amount at any level, however many dollars it is.

options.text: It falls, since higher-income households already spend a lot on recreation.
options.feedback: In this model the effect of a 1% rise depends only on β₁: a 1% rise always adds about 0.01 to ln(income), so spending rises by about $30 at any income.

practice.explanation: Section 9.3, Model 4: in y = β₀ + β₁ln(x), every 1% rise in x adds about β₁/100 to y, whatever the level of x.

practice.stem: Suppose a linear model of hourly wages gives wage = 4 + 1.5 × education, with wages in dollars and education in years. What is the predicted hourly wage of a worker with 16 years of education?

options.feedback: This is 1.5 × 16 without the intercept of 4.
This adds the intercept and the slope (4 + 1.5) without multiplying the slope by 16 years.
This multiplies the intercept by 16. The slope, not the intercept, is multiplied by years of education.

practice.explanation: Model 1 in Section 9.3: in a linear model the slope is a constant dollar change per year, and predictions add the intercept: 4 + 1.5 × 16 = $28.00.

practice.stem: Suppose four models of house price on lot size give these R² values: linear 0.40, log-linear 0.45, log-log 0.48, and linear-log 0.38. For which pairs of models is a comparison of R² a valid way to judge which fits better? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Log-log (0.48) and linear (0.40)
options.feedback: These models explain different dependent variables (ln(price) vs. price), so their R² values are not directly comparable.

options.text: Log-log (0.48) and log-linear (0.45)
options.feedback: Correct: both explain ln(price), so their R² values can be compared.

options.text: Linear (0.40) and linear-log (0.38)
options.feedback: Correct: both explain price in levels, so their R² values can be compared.

options.text: Log-linear (0.45) and linear (0.40)
options.feedback: One model explains ln(price) and the other price, so the R² values measure shares of different variations.

options.text: Linear-log (0.38) and log-log (0.48)
options.feedback: The linear-log model explains price and the log-log model ln(price), so their R² values are not comparable.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.5: compare R² only across models with the same dependent variable. Levels models are compared with levels models, log models with log models.

practice.stem: Suppose a dataset on 500 firms has mean annual sales of $8 million and median sales of $2 million, and every firm has positive sales. Which features support modeling ln(sales) rather than sales? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The mean is far above the median, a sign of a right-skewed distribution.
options.feedback: Correct: right-skewed variables such as sales are a standard reason to use logs.

options.text: Sales are measured in dollars, and any variable in dollars must be logged.
options.feedback: The unit of measurement does not decide the question; many dollar variables are modeled in levels.

options.text: Every firm has positive sales, so the log is defined for all of them.
options.feedback: Correct: logs require strictly positive values.

options.text: The dataset is large, with 500 firms.
options.feedback: Sample size does not determine the functional form.

options.text: The research question asks about percentage differences in sales.
options.feedback: Correct: when theory or the question is about percentage effects, a log dependent variable is natural.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.5 and the Key Takeaways: logs are natural for right-skewed, strictly positive variables and when the question concerns percentage effects.

practice.concept: Using logarithmic transformations (Key Takeaways, Key Concept 9.5)
practice.stem: Suppose some households in a survey report zero spending on tobacco, and spending is the dependent variable. Which model can be estimated on all households, including those with zero spending?

options.text: The log-linear model, with ln(spending) as the dependent variable
options.feedback: ln(0) is undefined, so households with zero spending would be dropped.

options.text: The log-log model, with ln(spending) as the dependent variable
options.feedback: ln(0) is undefined, so households with zero spending would be dropped.

options.text: None of the models, since a zero dependent variable must be dropped from any regression.
options.feedback: Zeros are fine in a levels regression; only the logarithm of zero is undefined.

options.text: The linear model, with spending in levels
options.feedback: Correct: spending in levels can be zero, while ln(spending) is undefined at zero.

practice.explanation: Key Takeaways: logs cannot be used when variables can be zero or negative, because ln(x) is defined only for x > 0.

practice.stem: Suppose a researcher wants to estimate the percentage change in a firm's sales associated with each additional year of the firm's age. Which specification answers this question directly?

options.text: Linear: sales = β₀ + β₁ × age
options.feedback: The linear model gives a dollar change in sales per year, not a percentage change.

options.text: Log-linear: ln(sales) = β₀ + β₁ × age
options.feedback: Correct: 100 × β₁ is the approximate percentage change in sales for one more year of age.

options.text: Log-log: ln(sales) = β₀ + β₁ × ln(age)
options.feedback: The log-log slope gives the percentage change in sales for a 1% change in age, not for one more year.

options.text: Linear-log: sales = β₀ + β₁ × ln(age)
options.feedback: The linear-log model gives a dollar change in sales for a 1% change in age.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.5: match the model to the question. A percentage change in y per unit of x is a semi-elasticity, estimated by the log-linear model.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of the log of a country's real GDP on the year gives ln(GDP) = 2.1 + 0.021 × year. What is the approximate average annual growth rate of GDP?

options.text: About 0.021% per year
options.feedback: The slope 0.021 is a proportionate change; multiply by 100 to express it as a percentage.

options.text: About 21% per year
options.feedback: This multiplies by 1,000 instead of 100.

options.text: About 2.1% per year
options.feedback: Correct: in ln(x) = β₀ + β₁ × t, the slope approximates the growth rate r, here 0.021, or about 2.1%.

options.text: About 0.021 units of GDP per year
options.feedback: The dependent variable is ln(GDP), so the slope is a growth rate, not a change in the level of GDP.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.6: regressing ln(x) on time linearizes exponential growth, and the slope approximates the constant growth rate (0.021 ≈ 2.1% per year).

practice.stem: If a country's GDP grows at a constant 3% per year, a plot of ln(GDP) against the year is close to a straight line.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. ln(x<sub>t</sub>) = ln(x₀) + ln(1.03) × t, which is linear in t with slope ln(1.03) ≈ 0.03.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 9.6: what happens to an exponential path after taking logs?

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.6: exponential growth in levels becomes linear growth in logs, which is why ln(x) can be regressed on time.

practice.stem: Suppose a city's population doubles in about 24 years. Using the Rule of 72, approximately what annual growth rate does this imply?

options.text: About 0.3% per year
options.feedback: This divides 24 by 72. The Rule of 72 gives doubling time = 72 ÷ growth rate, so growth rate = 72 ÷ doubling time.

options.text: About 4.2% per year
options.feedback: This divides 100 by 24. The rule uses 72.

options.text: About 0.03% per year
options.feedback: 72 ÷ 24 = 3 is already the growth rate in percent; it is not divided by 100 again.

options.text: About 3% per year
options.feedback: Correct: 72 ÷ 24 = 3, so the population grows at about 3% per year.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.7: doubling time ≈ 72 / r with r in percent, so r ≈ 72 / doubling time = 72 / 24 = 3%.

practice.stem: By the Rule of 72, a series growing at 2% per year takes about four times as long to double as one growing at 4% per year.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the formula in Key Concept 9.7 and compute both doubling times.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. 72/2 = 36 years versus 72/4 = 18 years: halving the growth rate doubles the doubling time.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 9.7: doubling time ≈ 72 / r is inversely proportional to the growth rate, so halving r (4% → 2%) doubles the doubling time (18 → 36 years).

exam.stem: The chapter's S&P 500 index was 17.66 in 1927 and 3,230.78 in 2019. Which expression equals ln(3,230.78) − ln(17.66)?

options.feedback: Revisit the properties of the natural logarithm listed in Section 9.1.
Revisit the properties of the natural logarithm listed in Section 9.1.
Correct. By the quotient rule, ln(a) − ln(b) = ln(a/b).
Revisit the difference between an exact equality and the approximation in Key Concept 9.1.

exam.explanation: Section 9.1 (quotient rule): ln(a/b) = ln(a) − ln(b), so the log difference equals ln(3,230.78/17.66) ≈ 5.21. The proportionate change (3,230.78 − 17.66)/17.66 is about 182, far from 5.21, because the log approximation works only for small changes.

exam.stem: Which of the following are correct properties of the natural logarithm, for positive numbers a, b, and x? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedback: Correct: e⁰ = 1, so ln(1) = 0.

options.text: ln(a + b) = ln(a) + ln(b)
options.feedback: Revisit the list of key properties in Section 9.1 and test the statement with simple numbers.

options.text: ln(aᵏ) = k × ln(a)
options.feedback: Correct: this is the power rule.

options.text: exp(ln(x)) = x
options.feedback: Correct: the exponential function undoes the logarithm.

options.text: ln(e) = 0
options.feedback: Revisit the list of key properties in Section 9.1.

exam.explanation: Section 9.1: ln(1) = 0, ln(e) = 1, ln(ab) = ln(a) + ln(b), ln(a/b) = ln(a) − ln(b), ln(aᵇ) = b × ln(a), and exp(ln(x)) = x. There is no rule for the log of a sum.

exam.stem: The natural logarithm of any number between 0 and 1, such as ln(0.5), is negative.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. ln(1) = 0 and ln(x) increases with x, so ln(x) < 0 for 0 < x < 1; for example, ln(0.5) ≈ −0.693.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the table of ln(x) values in Section 9.1, starting with x = 0.5.

exam.explanation: Section 9.1: the chapter's table shows ln(0.5) ≈ −0.693, ln(1) = 0, and ln(2) ≈ 0.693. Numbers below 1 have negative logs.

exam.concept: Logarithmic approximation of proportionate change (Section 9.1, Key Concept 9.1)
exam.stem: Suppose a worker's earnings rise from $40,000 to $60,000, an exact increase of 50%. Using 100 × [ln(60,000) − ln(40,000)], what percentage change would you compute, and how does it compare with the exact change?

options.text: About 40.5%, well below the exact 50% change
options.feedback: Correct: 100 × ln(1.5) ≈ 40.5%. For a change this large the log approximation understates the exact percentage change.

options.text: About 50%, equal to the exact change
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 9.1: how 100 × Δln(x) compares with the exact percentage change for a change of this size.

options.text: About 64.9%, well above the exact 50% change
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 9.1: how 100 × Δln(x) compares with the exact percentage change for a change of this size.

options.text: About 0.41%, well below the exact 50% change
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 9.1: how 100 × Δln(x) compares with the exact percentage change for a change of this size.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.1: 100 × Δln(x) ≈ %Δx is excellent for changes under about 10%. Here 100 × ln(60,000/40,000) = 100 × ln(1.5) ≈ 40.5%, well below the exact 50%.

exam.stem: Which ratio defines the semi-elasticity of earnings with respect to education?

options.text: (Δearnings / earnings) ÷ Δeducation
options.feedback: Correct. A semi-elasticity is the proportionate change in y per unit change in x.

options.text: (Δearnings / earnings) ÷ (Δeducation / education)
options.feedback: Revisit the definitions in Section 9.2 and Key Concept 9.2.

options.text: Δearnings ÷ Δeducation
options.feedback: Revisit the definitions in Section 9.2 and Key Concept 9.2.

options.text: Δearnings ÷ (Δeducation / education)
options.feedback: Revisit the definitions in Section 9.2 and Key Concept 9.2.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.2: semi-elasticity = (Δy/y)/Δx, a proportionate change in y per unit change in x; elasticity = (Δy/y)/(Δx/x). Multiplying the semi-elasticity by 100 gives the percentage change in y for a one-unit change in x.

exam.stem: Suppose a study finds that a 1% rise in the price of coffee is associated with a 0.4% fall in the quantity of coffee demanded, and that each additional year of work experience is associated with 3% higher wages. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The price elasticity of demand for coffee is about −0.4.
options.feedback: Correct: a percentage change in quantity per 1% change in price is an elasticity.

options.text: A $1 rise in the price of coffee is associated with a fall of 0.4 units in the quantity demanded.
options.feedback: Revisit whether each number in the stem compares percentage changes or changes in units (Section 9.2).

options.text: Both numbers are elasticities, since both describe percentage changes in the outcome.

exam.stem: For the 171 women in the earnings data, the log-linear model is ln(earnings) = 8.561 + 0.1314 × education. Which interpretation of 0.1314 is correct?

options.text: Each additional year of education is associated with earnings about $0.13 higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-linear model is interpreted (Key Concept 9.3).

options.text: A 1% increase in education is associated with earnings about 0.13% higher.

options.text: Each additional year of education is associated with earnings about 13.1% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-linear model, 100 × β₁ ≈ the percentage change in y for a one-unit increase in x.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.3: in ln(y) = β₀ + β₁x, the slope is a semi-elasticity, and 100 × 0.1314 ≈ 13.1% higher earnings per additional year of education (an approximation).

exam.stem: In the chapter's log-linear earnings model, the education coefficient is 0.1314, so two more years of education raise predicted ln(earnings) by 2 × 0.1314 = 0.2628. Computed exactly rather than with the approximation, the percentage difference in predicted earnings is closest to which value?

options.feedback: Revisit the exact formula in Key Concept 9.3.
Revisit the exact formula in Key Concept 9.3.
Revisit the exact formula in Key Concept 9.3.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.3: the exact percentage change is 100 × (e^Δln(y) − 1) = 100 × (e^0.2628 − 1) ≈ 30.1%. The approximation 100 × 0.2628 ≈ 26.3% understates it, and the gap grows with the size of the log change; exact effects also compound across years rather than add.

exam.stem: In the chapter's log-linear earnings model, one more year of education is associated with the same predicted dollar gain whether a worker's predicted earnings are $30,000 or $60,000.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the remark in Key Concept 9.3 that a percentage interpretation 'scales automatically'.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The log-linear model implies the same percentage gain at both levels, which is twice as many dollars at $60,000 as at $30,000.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.3: a log-linear model implies a constant percentage effect, so the implied dollar effect is proportional to the earnings level (about $3,900 at $30,000 and about $7,900 at $60,000 with the 13.1% approximation). A constant dollar effect is the linear model.

exam.stem: In the log-linear earnings model, the education coefficient 0.1314 has a standard error of 0.0143, a t-statistic of 9.21, and a p-value below 0.001. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Education explains about 92% of the variation in log earnings.
options.feedback: Revisit what a t-statistic measures, as opposed to R² (Section 9.3).

options.text: The slope is too small to matter, since 0.1314 is close to zero.
options.feedback: Revisit how the size of a log-linear slope is translated into an economic effect (Key Concept 9.3).

options.text: The slope is statistically significant at any conventional level, since p < 0.001.
options.feedback: Correct. With t = 9.21 and p < 0.001, H₀: β₁ = 0 is rejected at any conventional level.

options.text: The estimate proves that each extra year of education causes higher earnings.
options.feedback: Revisit what a significant regression slope in observational data does and does not show (Section 9.3).

exam.explanation: Section 9.3: t = b / se(b) = 9.21 (computed from unrounded values; p < 0.001), so the association is highly significant, i.e., very unlikely to reflect sampling variation alone. Significance is not causation, and R² (0.334) is a separate measure of fit.

exam.stem: The chapter's log-log model is ln(earnings) = 6.543 + 1.478 × ln(education). Which interpretation of 1.478 is correct?

options.text: Each additional year of education is associated with earnings about 1.48% higher.

options.text: A 1% increase in earnings is associated with about 1.48% more education.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-log model is interpreted (Key Concept 9.4).

options.text: A 1% increase in education is associated with earnings about 1.48% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-log model the slope is the elasticity: the percentage change in y for a 1% change in x.

options.text: A 1% increase in education is associated with earnings about 148% higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-log model is interpreted (Key Concept 9.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.4: in ln(y) = β₀ + β₁ln(x), β₁ = %Δy/%Δx is the elasticity. A 1% increase in education is associated with about 1.48% higher earnings.

exam.stem: The most educated workers in the earnings data have 20 years of education. For such a worker, a '1% increase in education' in the log-log model corresponds to about how many additional years of schooling?

options.text: About 1 year
options.feedback: Revisit the note on what a '1% increase in education' means in the log-log model (Section 9.3).

options.text: About 0.2 years
options.feedback: Correct: 1% of 20 years is 0.01 × 20 = 0.2 years, a fraction of a school year.

options.text: About 0.01 years
options.feedback: Revisit the note on what a '1% increase in education' means in the log-log model (Section 9.3).

options.text: About 2 years
options.feedback: Revisit the note on what a '1% increase in education' means in the log-log model (Section 9.3).

exam.explanation: Section 9.3 (Model 3): a 1% change is proportional to the starting level, here 0.01 × 20 = 0.2 years (about 0.14 years at the average of 14.4 years). This is why the chapter calls a '1% increase in education' a bit artificial.

exam.stem: In the log-log earnings model, the coefficient on ln(education) is 1.478. Using the log approximation, what percentage gain in earnings does the model imply for one more year of education for a worker with 12 years and for a worker with 18 years?

options.text: About 1.5% at both education levels
options.feedback: Revisit what percentage increase in education one more year represents at each level (Section 9.3, Model 3).

options.text: About 8.3% at 12 years and about 5.6% at 18 years
options.feedback: Revisit what percentage increase in education one more year represents at each level (Section 9.3, Model 3).

options.text: About 17.7% at 12 years and about 26.6% at 18 years
options.feedback: Revisit what percentage increase in education one more year represents at each level (Section 9.3, Model 3).

options.text: About 12.3% at 12 years and about 8.2% at 18 years
options.feedback: Correct: 147.8/12 ≈ 12.3% at 12 years and 147.8/18 ≈ 8.2% at 18 years.

exam.explanation: Section 9.3: the log-log model implies a percentage return to an extra year of about 100 × β₁ / education: 147.8/12 ≈ 12.3% at 12 years and 147.8/18 ≈ 8.2% at 18 years, so the percentage return falls as education rises.

exam.stem: The slope of the chapter's log-log earnings model would stay the same if education were measured in months instead of years.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Multiplying education by 12 adds the constant ln(12) to ln(education), which shifts the intercept but leaves the slope unchanged.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the remark in Key Concept 9.4 about units of measurement.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.4: an elasticity is unit-free. ln(12 × education) = ln(12) + ln(education), so a change of units changes only the intercept.

exam.stem: The chapter's linear-log model is earnings = −102,767 + 54,452 × ln(education). Approximately how much higher are predicted annual earnings when education rises by 1%?

options.text: About $545
options.feedback: Correct: in a linear-log model, a 1% increase in x changes y by about β₁/100 = 54,452/100 ≈ $545.

options.text: About $54,452
options.feedback: Revisit how the linear-log slope is scaled for a 1% change in x (Section 9.3, Model 4).

options.text: About $5,445

exam.explanation: Section 9.3, Model 4: in y = β₀ + β₁ln(x), a 1% increase in x changes ln(x) by about 0.01, so y changes by about β₁/100 = 54,452/100 ≈ $545.

exam.stem: In the chapter's linear-log earnings model, how does the predicted dollar gain in earnings from one more year of education change as a worker's education rises?

options.text: It stays at about $5,021 per year at every level of education.
options.feedback: Revisit which model implies a constant dollar gain per year (Section 9.3).

options.text: It stays the same at every level, since the model is linear in its coefficients.
options.feedback: Revisit how education enters the linear-log model (Section 9.3, Model 4).

options.text: It rises, since workers with more education earn more.
options.feedback: Revisit what the slope multiplies in the linear-log model (Section 9.3, Model 4).

options.text: It falls, since each extra year adds less and less to ln(education) as education grows.
options.feedback: Correct. ln(education) rises by less for each additional year as education grows (for example, ln(13) − ln(12) ≈ 0.080 but ln(19) − ln(18) ≈ 0.054), so each year adds fewer dollars.

exam.explanation: Section 9.3: the linear-log model captures diminishing returns. ln(education) rises more slowly as education grows, so each additional year adds fewer dollars.

exam.stem: The chapter's linear model is earnings = −31,056 + 5,021 × education. By how much do predicted annual earnings differ between a worker with 18 years and a worker with 12 years of education?

options.feedback: Revisit how the linear model is used to compare predictions at two education levels (Section 9.3, Model 1).
Revisit how the linear model is used to compare predictions at two education levels (Section 9.3, Model 1).
Revisit how the linear model is used to compare predictions at two education levels (Section 9.3, Model 1).
Correct: the intercept cancels, so the gap is 5,021 × (18 − 12) = 5,021 × 6 = $30,126.

exam.explanation: Section 9.3, Model 1: the linear model implies a constant dollar gain per year, so the gap is 5,021 × 6 = $30,126 whatever the starting level. Practice Exercise 6 compares this with the log-linear model.

exam.stem: The chapter reports R² = 0.289 for the linear model, 0.334 for the log-linear model, 0.286 for the log-log model, and 0.230 for the linear-log model. Which comparisons are valid? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The log-linear model fits better than the linear model, since 0.334 > 0.289.
options.feedback: Revisit when R² values from different specifications can be compared (Key Concept 9.5).

options.text: The log-linear model fits better than the log-log model, since 0.334 > 0.286.
options.feedback: Correct: both models explain ln(earnings), so their R² values can be compared.

options.feedback: Correct: both models explain earnings in dollars, so their R² values can be compared.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.5: R² is comparable only across models with the same dependent variable. Among the ln(earnings) models the log-linear fits best (0.334 vs. 0.286); among the earnings models the linear fits best (0.289 vs. 0.230).

exam.stem: In the chapter's earnings example, which of the following support modeling ln(earnings) rather than earnings? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Earnings are right-skewed: the mean (about $41,413) is well above the median ($36,000).
options.feedback: Correct: a long upper tail is a standard reason to use logs.

options.text: Every worker has positive earnings (the minimum is $1,050), so the log is defined for all of them.
options.feedback: Correct: logs require strictly positive values.

options.text: The linear model's slope is highly significant (t = 8.30), which calls for a log transformation.
options.feedback: Revisit the criteria listed in Key Concept 9.5 for choosing a functional form.

options.text: Theories of the returns to schooling are usually stated in percentage terms.
options.feedback: Correct: when theory predicts percentage effects, a log dependent variable is natural.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.5: data properties (a right-skewed, strictly positive dependent variable) and economic theory (percentage returns to schooling) both point to ln(earnings). Statistical significance of a slope is not a criterion for the functional form.

exam.concept: Using logarithmic transformations (Key Takeaways, Key Concept 9.5)

options.text: Only the log-linear and the log-log models

options.feedback: Correct: both use ln(education), which is undefined at 0 years of education.

exam.explanation: Key Takeaways: logs are not usable when a variable can be zero, because ln(0) is undefined. The log-log and linear-log models use ln(education); the linear and log-linear models use education in years. (In the actual data, education ranges from 3 to 20 years.)

exam.stem: The chapter regresses the log of the S&P 500 index on the year (93 annual observations, 1927–2019): ln(sp500) = −124.09 + 0.0653 × year. What does the slope imply?

options.text: The index grew by about 6.5% per year on average over 1927–2019.
options.feedback: Correct: in ln(x) = β₀ + β₁ × t, the slope approximates the constant growth rate.

options.text: The index grew by about 0.065% per year on average.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a regression of ln(x) on time is interpreted (Key Concept 9.6).

options.text: The index rose by about 6.5 points per year on average.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a regression of ln(x) on time is interpreted (Key Concept 9.6).

options.text: The index rose by about 0.065 points per year on average.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a regression of ln(x) on time is interpreted (Key Concept 9.6).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.6: regressing ln(x) on time linearizes exponential growth, and the slope approximates the growth rate r: 0.0653 ≈ 6.5% per year (strictly, the slope estimates ln(1 + r), so the exact rate is e<sup>0.0653</sup> − 1 ≈ 6.75%).

exam.stem: If the S&P 500 grew at a roughly constant percentage rate, a plot of the index itself (not its logarithm) against the year would be close to a straight line.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the two panels comparing the index in levels and in logs (Section 9.4).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Constant percentage growth adds ever larger amounts in levels, so the levels plot curves upward; it is the plot of ln(sp500) that is close to a straight line.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.6: exponential growth in levels is linear in logs. The chapter's levels plot is an upward-bending curve, while ln(sp500) against year is nearly a straight line (R² = 0.958).

exam.stem: Suppose an economy's real GDP per capita grows at a steady 2.4% per year. Using the Rule of 72, approximately how many years does it take to double?

options.text: About 3,000 years
options.feedback: Revisit the doubling-time formula in Key Concept 9.7.

options.text: About 30 years
options.feedback: Correct: 72 ÷ 2.4 = 30 years.

options.text: About 173 years
options.feedback: Revisit the doubling-time formula in Key Concept 9.7.

options.text: About 42 years
options.feedback: Revisit the doubling-time formula in Key Concept 9.7.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.7: doubling time ≈ 72 / r, with r in percent: 72 / 2.4 = 30 years.

exam.stem: By the Rule of 72, a country with GDP per capita of $5,000 and a country with GDP per capita of $50,000, both growing at 3% per year, take about the same number of years to double.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The doubling time 72/r depends only on the growth rate: about 24 years for both countries.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the formula in Key Concept 9.7: which quantities does the doubling time depend on?

exam.explanation: Key Concept 9.7: doubling time ≈ 72 / r depends only on the growth rate, not on the starting level. At 3%, both double in about 72/3 = 24 years.
